SUIT FOR SPECIFIC PERFORMANCE (MAIN SUIT)
 SUIT FOR CANCELLATION (CONNECTED SUIT)
 JUDGMENT 1.

This court is rendering the present common judgment to adjudicate two suits, firstly the suit filed on 23.05.1988 by the plaintiff against the defendants for specific performance of the agreement dated 09.02.1988 entered into between the parties and secondly, suit filed on 15.04.1988 by the defendant against the plaintiff for cancelling the agreement to sell dated 23.05.1988 and receipt dated 09.02.1988, respectively.

It is pertinent to mention that the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi vide order Judgment Page No. 8 of 114 dated 09.05.2025 M DJ No. 61199/2015 (Main Suit) CNR No. :

Plaintiff has alleged that the defendant after executing the agreement started negotiating with other parties as well and therefore, on 15.02.1988, the plaintiff approached the defendant and requested not to enter into agreement with any other person, qua the suit property, though, the defendant refused the request of the plaintiff.

5. Plaintiff has further averred that keeping in view the circumstances a suit bearing no. 88 of 1988 was filed by the plaintiff for grant of permanent injunction, wherein the defendant denied the execution of the agreement dated 09.02.1988 and contended that he took loan of .50,000/- from the plaintiff.

A legal notice dated 16.03.1988 was served upon the defendant for honouring the agreement dated 09.02.1988, the same was received by the defendant but allegedly defendant did not honour the terms of the agreement.

Facts pleaded in written statement of defendant (In brief)
8.

The defendant has taken a stand that since his wife was negotiating to purchase the plot no. A/55, G Block, Ramditta Enclave, Village Posangipur, Delhi for Rs. 46000/-
and for this purpose the defendant approached the plaintiff, who was the tenant of the defendant,
for taking monetary help.

The plaintiff has denied all the allegations made in the written statement and reiterated the averments of the plaint and sought the decree in the present suit.
Circumstances after the death of the defendant 13.

The defendant died on 07.12.2004 and thereafter plaintiff has substituted his legal representatives on record vide order dated 10.05.2007, though defendant no.9 impleaded in the present suit by way of an application filed on 16.05.2005 under Order I Rule 10 CPC and he was allowed to file written statement vide order dated 04.06.2008.
In pursuance of the said order the defendant no.9 filed the written statement on 19.12.2008.
Subsequently, defendant no.6 and 7 proceeded as ex-parte vide order dated 27.02.2009, whereas on the application the court allowed the defendants no. 1 and 8 to file additional written statement.

sentences.text: At the outset it is necessary to explain and discuss the nature and scope of the principle of Res Judicata which is statutorily encapsulated in Section 11 of the CPC.

It is well settled that in order to decide whether a decision in an earlier litigation operates as R es Judicata , the court must look at the nature of the litigation, what the issues raised therein were, and what was actually decided in it.

When a matter, whether on a question of fact or on a question of law, has been decided between two parties in one suit or proceeding and the decision is final, either because no appeal was taken to a higher court or because the appeal was dismissed or no appeal lies, neither party will be allowed in a future suit or proceeding to canvass the matter again.
39. The term 'res judicata' means 'thing already decided by a competent court.'
Section 11 of CPC embodies the doctrine of Res Judicata in India.

It states that no Court shall try any suit or issue in which the issue directly and substantially, in a former suit, between the same parties or Judgment Page No. 28 of 114 dated 09.05.2025 M DJ No. 61199/2015 (Main Suit) CNR No. :

41. The fundamental rationale behind this principle is that every litigation must come to an end.

Once a final judgment has been announced in a suit, the Court in the subsequent matters if finds that it is identical to or substantially the same as the earlier suit then, it would apply the doctrine of Res Judicata to preserve the effect of the first judgment.
This is to prevent injustice to the parties of a case supposedly finished, but perhaps mostly to avoid unnecessary waste of resources and time of the Judicial System.
This is just to prevent them from multiplying judgments.
The doctrine seeks to prevent the determination of claims which were failed to be brought at the appropriate time in earlier proceedings.

50.
The law of Order II Rule 2 may be summed up as it is a provision enacted with a view to prevent the multiplicity of suits.
It will be right to say that it is based on the principle that a person should not be vexed twice for one and the same cause of action.
It is well established that it is a rule that dealt with two circumstances, i.e., the splitting up of claims and the splitting up of remedies.
Hence, it requires the inclusion of the whole claim arising in respect of one and the same cause of action in one suit.
However, it is not the mandate of the law that every suit shall include every claim or every cause of action that the plaintiff may have against the defendant.
51. Therefore, where the causes of action are different in the two suits, Order II Rule 2 would have no application.

The rule lucidly provides that Order II Rule 2 contemplates two different situations, namely, where a plaintiff omits or relinquishes a part of a claim that he is entitled to make and, secondly, where the plaintiff omits or relinquishes one out of the several reliefs that he could have claimed in the suit.

25 is only in the latter situation where the plaintiff can file a subsequent suit seeking the relief omitted in the earlier suit, provided that at the time of omission to claim the particular relief, he had obtained the leave of the court in the first suit.

Specific performance in respect of contracts.--The specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court subject to the provisions contained in subsection (2) of section 11, section 14 and section 16.
49.
This provision, which remained in the realm of the Courts' discretion, was converted into a mandatory provision, prescribing a power the Courts had to exercise when the ingredients were fulfilled.
This was a significant step in the growth of commercial law as the sanctity of contracts was reinforced with parties having to comply with contracts and thereby reducing efficient breaches.
50. Under the pre amended Specific Relief Act, one of the major considerations for grant of specific performance was the adequacy of damages under Section 14(1)(a).

However, this consideration has now been completely done away with, in order to provide better compensation to the aggrieved party in the form of specific performance.
51.

Having come to the conclusion that the 2018 amendment was not a mere procedural enactment,
rather it had substantive principles built into its working, this Court cannot hold that such amendments would apply retrospectively."

Prior to the amendment, this relief was discretionary in nature,
meaning the courts could decide whether to grant it based on equitable considerations, such as the availability of damages and a few other conditions, as a sufficient remedy.

101. The judgment also addressed the temporal applicability, i.e., whether it can be applied to past actions or events, of the amendments.

The Hon'ble Supreme Court made it clear that since the changes introduced by the 2018 amendment were substantive in nature, affecting the legal rights and obligations of the parties, they could not be applied retrospectively.

As a result, these amendments apply only to contracts and transactions executed after the commencement of the amendment and not to those that were already in existence or to legal proceedings that were pending before the amendment came into force.

102. This decision serves as a binding clarification that the 2018 amendments to the SRA cannot affect past or pending cases, and firmly establishes that specific performance has become a legal right, not merely an equitable remedy, in all future cases where the statutory conditions are fulfilled.

103. Thus, in the present matter, since the suit was already pending at the time when the 2018 amendments to the SRA came into force, the legal regime as it existed Judgment Page No. 62 of 114 dated 09.05.2025 M DJ No. 61199/2015 (Main Suit) CNR No. : DLCT01-004795-2015 Durga Devi Vs Kirpa Ram and CS DJ No. 11871/2016 (Connected Suit) CNR No. :DLCT01- 000005-1988 Kirpa Ram Vs Durga Devi & Anr.

10.Cases in which specific performance of contract enforceable.--
Except as otherwise provided in this Chapter, the specific performance of any contract may, in the discretion of the court, be enforced-- (a)when there exists no standard for ascertaining actual damage caused by the non- performance of the act agreed to be done; or(b)when the act agreed to be done is such that compensation in money for its non- performance would not afford adequate relief.

Explanation.--Unless and until the contrary is proved, the court shall presume-- (i)that the breach of a contract to transfer immovable property cannot be adequately relieved by compensation in money; and(ii)that the breach of a contract to transfer movable property can be so relieved except in the following cases:
(a)where the property is not an ordinary article of commerce, or is of special value or interest to the plaintiff, or consists of goods which are not easily obtainable in the market;
(b)where the property is held by the defendant as the agent or trustee of the plaintiff.

(i) where a contract involves the payment of money, it is not essential for the plaintiff to actually tender to the defendant or to deposit in court any money except when so directed by the court;

127. A reading of the highlighted portion of the said paragraph makes it abundantly clear concepts of "readiness" and "willingness" are inherently subjective and pertain directly to the mental resolve and intention of the plaintiff.
These aspects involve personal volition and state of mind, which cannot be delegated to or testified upon by any third party, including a constituted attorney.

128. The power of attorney holder, while competent to appear and depose in respect of matters within his personal knowledge or regarding acts done by him on behalf of the principal, cannot validly testify regarding the principal's mental state, personal conduct, or subjective readiness and willingness.

Since these elements are deeply rooted in the plaintiff's personal capacity and mental attitude, the power to prove such aspects cannot be delegated to another person, even if that person holds a power of attorney.

Except as otherwise provided by this Chapter, specific performance of a contract may be enforced against-- (a) xxxxxxxxxx......

Similarly, Section 52 of the TPA which provides the principle of lis pendens is mentioned here as under, that "52. Transfer of property pending suit relating thereto.-- During the [pendency] in any Court having authority [within the limits of India excluding the State of Jammu and Kashmir]
or established beyond such limits] by [the Central Government, of [any] suit or proceeding [which is not collusive and] in which any right to immovable property is directly and specifically in question,
the property cannot be transferred or otherwise dealt with by any party to the suit or proceeding so as to affect the rights of any other party thereto under any decree or order which may be made therein, except under the authority of the Court and on such terms as it may impose.

[Explanation.--For the purpose of this section, the pendency of a suit or proceeding shall be deemed to commence from the date of the presentation of the plaint or the institution of the proceeding in a court of competent jurisdiction, and to continue until the suit or proceeding has been disposed of by a final decree or order, and complete satisfaction or discharge of such decree or order has been obtained, or has become unobtainable by reason of the expiration of any period of limitation prescribed for the execution thereof by any law for the time being in force.]"

171. The basic rationale and fundamental object of the principle of lis pendens is for maintaining the status quo and no party is allowed to change it directly or indirectly during Judgment Page No. 97 of 114 dated 09.05.2025 M

65 2025.05.21 16:58:41 +0530 the pendency of the litigation.
The doctrine is based on the principle of equity and good conscience that aims to prevent the multiplicity of the litigation.

172. Whereas, Section 19 SRA mandates that the specific performance of an agreement may be enforced against any person or persons claiming under him save as a transferee for valuable consideration in good faith and that too without notice of the existing or prior agreement.
Though Section 19(b) SRA protects the bonafide purchaser in good faith for valuable consideration, the protection is in the nature of an exception to the general rule.
Therefore, the onus of proof of good faith is on the person who has taken a plea of bonafide purchaser.
Indeed, 'good faith" is only a factual issue that must be evaluated and determined in light of the particular facts and circumstances of each case.
173. Further, as per the Section 2(11) of the Bhartiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Section-152 IPC) defines "good faith", as any act which is done with due care and attention.

sentences.text: The principles specified in Section 52 of the TP Act are in accordance with equity, good conscience or justice because they rest upon an equitable and just foundation that it will be impossible to bring an action or suit to a successful termination if alienations are permitted to prevail.
A transferee pendente lite is bound by the decree just as much as he was a party to the suit.
The principle of lis pendens embodied in Section 52 of the TP Act being a principle of public policy, no question of good faith or bona fide arises.
The principle underlying Section 52 is that a litigating party is exempted from taking notice of a title acquired during the pendency of the litigation.
The mere pendency of a suit does not prevent one of the parties from dealing with the property constituting the subject- matter of the suit.

The section only postulates a condition that the alienation will in no manner affect the rights of the other party under any decree which may be passed in the suit unless the property was alienated with the permission of the court."

sentences.text: The Doctrine of Lis Pendens is based on the maxim "pendente lite nihil innovetur".
This means that pending litigation, nothing new should be introduced.
Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 (for short, 'the TP Act'), which incorporates the Doctrine of Lis Pendens, is based on equity and public policy.
It pours complete efficacy to the adjudicatory mechanism.

This is done by finding that any disposition of property, as described in the Section by a party to the litigation will, in not any way, detract from the finality of the decision rendered by the court.

It is clear that it is not based on the ground of Notice as laid down by Lord Craanworth in Bennamy v.
Sabine, which has been followed by the Privy Council in the decision in 34 Indian Appeals 102.
We may notice the following discussion in this regard in "The Transfer of Property, by Mulla, 12th Edition:
"The rule is, therefore, based not on the doctrine of notice, but on expediency, ie, the necessity for fine adjudication.

It is immaterial whether the alienee pendente lite had,
or had not, notice of the pending proceeding.

This is, of course, no longer the case in England, or in Gujarat and Maharashtra, where the doctrine only affects transactions pendente lite if the lis has been duly registered."

The same may be reproduced as under, "111. Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence.

Where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence."
Illustrations:
(a) The good faith of a sale by a client to an attorney is in question in a suit brought by the client.
The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the attorney.
(b) The good faith of a sale by a son just come of age to a father is in question in a suit brought by the son.
The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the father.
193. From the above referred to section it is clear that the duty of demonstrating good faith rests with the party in a position of active confidence over the other party.
It is settled law that a person in a fiduciary relationship has an obligation to safeguard the interests of the person entrusted to his care.
The court monitors all transactions between these parties to prevent the protector from abusing his power.

As a result, whenever suspicion arises in a particular set of circumstances, the law assumes everything against the transaction, and the burden of proof is placed on the person in the position of confidence or trust to demonstrate that the transaction is entirely fair and reasonable.

However, this Court cannot accept this explanation for the reason that if Sh. Kirpa Ram's sole intention was to sell the property to Defendant No. 9, then Ex.D9W1/25 could not be considered his last will and testament.
Furthermore, if Ex.D9W1/25 was indeed his last testament, then the transaction involving the sale of the suit property for 1,90,000 by Sh.Kirpa Ram to Defendant No. 9 becomes irrelevant.

The defendant asserts ownership of the property based on both the agreement to sell Ex.D9W1/3 and the Will Ex.D9W1/25 concurrently.

On one hand, he is claiming his right to the property as a bonafide purchaser and on the other hand, he is fighting a probate case of the Will Ex.D9W1/25 in which the same property allegedly was bequeathed to him by Sh. Kirpa Ram.

The claim of defendant no. 9 of the execution of two rival documents at the same time i.e. Ex.D9W1/3 (agreement to sell) and Ex.D9W1/25 (Will) by Sh. Kirpa Ram in favour of defendant no. 9 cannot be accepted by this Court.

200. In totality, defendant No. 9 has not successfully demonstrated that he is a bonafide purchaser,
as the property in question was purportedly transferred during the pendency of the current suit,
wherein an injunction order was already in effect, rendering the transaction illegal.

At the outset it is necessary to explain and discuss the nature and scope of the principle of Res Judicata which is statutorily encapsulated in Section 11 of the CPC.
It is well settled that in order to decide whether a decision in an earlier litigation operates as R es Judicata , the court must look at the nature of the litigation, what the issues raised therein were, and what was actually decided in it.
When a matter, whether on a question of fact or on a question of law, has been decided between two parties in one suit or proceeding and the decision is final, either because no appeal was taken to a higher court or because the appeal was dismissed or no appeal lies, neither party will be allowed in a future suit or proceeding to canvass the matter again.
39. The term 'res judicata' means 'thing already decided by a competent court.'
Section 11 of CPC embodies the doctrine of Res Judicata in India.
It states that no Court shall try any suit or issue in which the issue directly and substantially, in a former suit, between the same parties or Judgment Page No. 28 of 114 dated 09.05.2025 M DJ No. 61199/2015 (Main Suit) CNR No. :

The law of Order II Rule 2 may be summed up as it is a provision enacted with a view to prevent the multiplicity of suits.
It will be right to say that it is based on the principle that a person should not be vexed twice for one and the same cause of action.
It is well established that it is a rule that dealt with two circumstances, i.e., the splitting up of claims and the splitting up of remedies.
Hence, it requires the inclusion of the whole claim arising in respect of one and the same cause of action in one suit.
However, it is not the mandate of the law that every suit shall include every claim or every cause of action that the plaintiff may have against the defendant.
51. Therefore, where the causes of action are different in the two suits, Order II Rule 2 would have no application.
The rule lucidly provides that Order II Rule 2 contemplates two different situations, namely, where a plaintiff omits or relinquishes a part of a claim that he is entitled to make and, secondly, where the plaintiff omits or relinquishes one out of the several reliefs that he could have claimed in the suit.

The same may be reproduced as under, "111. Proof of good faith in transactions where one party is in relation of active confidence.
Where there is a question as to the good faith of a transaction between parties, one of whom stands to the other in a position of active confidence, the burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the party who is in a position of active confidence."
Illustrations:
(a) The good faith of a sale by a client to an attorney is in question in a suit brought by the client.
The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the attorney.
(b) The good faith of a sale by a son just come of age to a father is in question in a suit brought by the son.
The burden of proving the good faith of the transaction is on the father.
193. From the above referred to section it is clear that the duty of demonstrating good faith rests with the party in a position of active confidence over the other party.
It is settled law that a person in a fiduciary relationship has an obligation to safeguard the interests of the person entrusted to his care.
The court monitors all transactions between these parties to prevent the protector from abusing his power.
As a result, whenever suspicion arises in a particular set of circumstances, the law assumes everything against the transaction, and the burden of proof is placed on the person in the position of confidence or trust to demonstrate that the transaction is entirely fair and reasonable.

159. In legal proceedings, especially where the party seeks to establish conduct that supports a claim of readiness and willingness, it is imperative that assertions made in oral evidence are duly supported by contemporaneous documentary material.
The absence of such documents, particularly when they are within the exclusive possession and knowledge of the plaintiff, raises serious doubts about the truthfulness of the claims.
Moreover, the failure to mention even the approximate timeline of such critical actions further indicates a lack of credibility and suggests that these statements may have been made merely as an afterthought to bolster his case.
Thus, a third party who had no personal knowledge cannot give evidence about such readiness and willingness, even if he is an attorney holder of the person concerned.
It has also nowhere been pleaded that the husband of the plaintiff had all the requisite knowledge about the facts of the case and also about the readiness and willingness of the plaintiff to buy the suit property.
Though Section 19(b) SRA protects the bonafide purchaser in good faith for valuable consideration, the protection is in the nature of an exception to the general rule.
Therefore, the onus of proof of good faith is on the person who has taken a plea of bonafide purchaser.
Indeed, 'good faith" is only a factual issue that must be evaluated and determined in light of the particular facts and circumstances of each case.
Therefore, the alleged transaction is clearly falls within the ambit of Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act (hereinafter to be referred to as 'TPA') which incorporates the doctrine of lis pendens.
